title: Jim Cramer doubles down on his stock market stand
detail:
Jim Cramer doubles down on his stock market stand
Hillary Remy, Dana Sullivan Kilroy
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 11:47 AM MST 6 min read
^GSPC
^IXIC
^DJI
CL=F

Markets posted broad losses on Oct. 14, with the S&P 500 falling just over 1%, the Nasdaq dropping 1.9% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closing modestly lower. The declines came as investors weighed a hotter-than-expected inflation report, rising oil prices and growing uncertainty around Federal Reserve policy.

The session offered few clear signals. Strong quarterly results from two widely followed companies failed to support their shares, Treasury yields moved in ways that contradicted historical patterns, and geopolitical risk added another layer of pressure. Jim Cramer watched all of it and offered a direct response.

The CNBC host told investors to stay in the market. He argued that attempting to time an exit during a confusing stretch could prove far more costly than riding out the volatility.

Also read: Jim Cramer spots something investors may be missing on Wall Street

Why staying invested matters

The foundation of Cramer's argument was JPMorgan Chase research tracking S&P 500 returns over a 20-year period. An investor who put $10,000 into the index in 2005 and stayed fully invested through 2024 would have accumulated substantially more than one who missed the index's 10 best trading days across those two decades.

The gap was not small. The investor who sat out just those 10 sessions ended with less than half the wealth of the one who stayed in throughout. Those best days, Cramer noted, rarely announce themselves in advance.

Investors who sell during a downturn often do so to prevent further losses. The sharpest single-day gains, though, tend to arrive during the same stretches of peak volatility. That is when sitting out the market feels like the only reasonable move.

Cramer said investors who "throw things away and go home" face a harder problem than avoiding further declines. Buying back in after a sharp recovery means paying more than an investor who never left, and the timing of that recovery is rarely predictable.

Cramer said the conflicting data makes it difficult to gauge what the Fed will do next.John Lamparski / Getty Images
Inflation is sending mixed signals

The September consumer price index rose 0.6% from the prior month, above analyst estimates. The report sent Treasury yields higher initially as investors priced in a more aggressive Federal Reserve response to the hotter-than-expected reading.

Yields reversed later in the session even as oil prices continued to climb. The divergence was notable. Hotter inflation typically keeps yields elevated by sustaining expectations for higher interest rates, but that relationship broke down Oct. 14 as bonds recovered ground.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2% to 26,174.2, and the S&P 500 declined 1.1% to 7,660.5 after midday Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.4% to 51,955.7, after trading higher earlier in the session.

Technology, communication services and consumer discretionary were among the worst performers. Energy, utilities, and consumer staples topped the gainers. Technology is poised to hit the bottom of sector charts this week, while consumer defensive is emerging as the leader.

CoreWeave (CRWV) co-founders Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo and Brannin McBee have sold $3.3 billion in company shares since its March 2025 initial public offering, including $2.4 billion in 2026, Bloomberg reported. Shares sank over 12%, extending losses from earlier this week as concern mounted around its debt and credit risk.

The PHLX Semiconductor slumped 2.8%, sliding for the eighth straight day amid jitters surrounding the so-called AI trade. Seventeen of the bottom 20 names among stocks with market capitalization exceeding $200 billion were from the technology sector, according to data compiled by Finviz. Palo Alto Networks (PANW) led decliners, down 7.7%.

In geopolitical news, President Donald Trump said the US may have to target Iran's Pickaxe Mountain as he seeks to ensure Tehran does not get a nuclear weapon, Reuters reported.

Iranian Acting Oil Minister Hamid Bovard has said the country "will take precise, appropriate retaliatory measures at the right time to counter enemy threats" to its energy facilities, Al Jazeera, a Middle Eastern broadcaster, reported.

The front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil contract jumped 3.1% to $101.00 per barrel, while global benchmark Brent advanced 3.3% to $109.38 per barrel.

In economic news, industrial production rose 0.7% in September, versus expectations for 0.4% in a Bloomberg-compiled poll, and following an upwardly revised 0.1% increase in August, according to the Federal Reserve.

The New York Federal Reserve's services index fell to minus 20.7 in October from minus 8.7 in September, compared with the minus 4.1 forecast in a survey compiled by Bloomberg. The index is the first services sector reading for October and suggests widespread contraction.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh avoided signaling the Fed's next monetary policy moves but reaffirmed its commitment to price stability, according to a Commerzbank note. Warsh, however, sees a significant investment boom driven by artificial intelligence, per the research note.

US Treasury yields were mixed, with the two-year rate steady at 4.76%. The 10-year yield rose 2.5 basis points to 5.11%, and the 30-year rate climbed two basis points to 5.45%.

title: The Stock Market Has Seen This Happen Only 2 Other Times in Over 150 Years, and History Has an Ominous Warning for Investors
detail:
The Stock Market Has Seen This Happen Only 2 Other Times in Over 150 Years, and History Has an Ominous Warning for Investors
Geoffrey Seiler, The Motley Fool

^GSPC
NVDA

Trading disclosure

The stock market is entering the fifth year of the current bull market, which started in October 2022. During these past four years, the S&P 500 has surged nearly 120%, fueled by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

However, the question on many investors' minds is how much longer the good times can last. There are certainly signs the bull market could be losing steam. The breadth of market winners is actually quite narrow, with only a handful of stocks helping power the index. In fact, over a quarter of stocks in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) are actually down 40% or more from their all-time highs, while nearly 60% of S&P 500 stocks are below their 200-day moving average.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Meanwhile, renowned investors like Michael Burry, who correctly called the housing bubble, and billionaire hedge fund manager Ray Dalio have been predicting that the AI bubble will burst. Burry has been very vocal, shorting several popular AI stocks, including Nvidia, Micron Technology, and Palantir Technologies, while comparing the current market to before the 2000 dot-com bubble. Dalio, meanwhile, has said the AI boom shows classic signs of a bubble ready to burst.

Image source: Getty Images.

One of the strongest indicators that the current bull market could be coming to an end is the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio. Created by Yale economist Robert Shiller in 1988, it measures the value of the S&P index relative to its 10-year average inflation-adjusted earnings. The purpose of this is to smooth out periods of earnings boom and bust cycles.

The valuation metric currently sits above 40, which is its second-highest level ever. The only two other times the CAPE ratio has moved above 32 were right before the Great Depression in 1929, when it reached 32.6, and during the dot-com bubble, when it peaked at 44.2. Both times the CAPE hit these levels, huge market corrections followed.

Shiller CAPE Ratio data by YCharts

How investors should prepare for a potential market correction

Given the current warning signs in the market, it may seem like the common-sense thing to do would be to sell stocks and step to the sidelines. However, this would likely be a bad decision, as trying to time the stock market rarely works, and even if it does, then you'd have to correctly time getting back in as well. Miss out on some of the largest days in the stock market, and your investment returns could suffer significantly.

Worry that tech giants may slow spending on optical hardware sent Applied Optoelectronics (NASDAQ:AAOI) down 23.6% this week, extending a drop that leaves shares down 64.2% (as of the close on Thursday, Oct. 15) from their 52-week high.

Applied Optoelectronics stock changed hands at $83.73 as of the close on Thursday, Oct. 15, down 23.6% from Friday, Oct. 9's close through Thursday, Oct. 15's close. Across those five sessions, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 0.9%, the Nasdaq-100 dropped 3.1%, and the Technology Select Sector (NYSEMKT:XLK) lost 4.8%.

Image source: Getty Images.

AI infrastructure spending fears hit optical component makers

Broadcom CEO Hock Tan warned that capital access and funding constraints could slow the build-out of artificial intelligence infrastructure. That warning triggered a sell-off across photonics component makers, hitting Applied Optoelectronics harder than peers like Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE) and Coherent (NYSE:COHR). The stock had reached a 52-week high of $233.67 before falling, and it remains down 64.2% (as of the close on Thursday, Oct. 15) from that peak. The drop follows the company's completion of a $600 million at-the-market equity offering, which raised liquidity to expand manufacturing capacity for 800G optical transceivers but also contributed to shareholder dilution. B. Riley also lowered its price target on the stock to $92 from $109.

Applied Optoelectronics manufactures optical networking components, like transceivers and lasers, for internet data centers and cable television operators. The company's higher-speed 800G optical transceivers are designed to handle high-density data traffic inside AI server clusters. However, customer concentration remains a vulnerability, with its top 10 customers accounting for 99% of total revenue.

In its last reported quarter, which ended June 30, 2026, revenue jumped 86.4% year over year to $191.9 million, driven by data center demand, while the company posted a $22.8 million net loss. Management has been expanding manufacturing facilities in Texas to meet projected demand for next-generation optical modules. This week's optical sector sell-off sharpens concerns that funding constraints among major cloud customers could slow Applied Optoelectronics' rapid capacity expansion.

The stock trades at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 11.9, a valuation that reflects high growth expectations for its high-speed optical components. With cash and short-term investments totaling $509 million as of June 30, 2026, and total debt of $93 million, the company has sufficient cash to fund capital expenditure plans. However, ongoing GAAP losses leave the multiple vulnerable if revenue growth slows.

U.S. equities continue to show resilience despite a volatile backdrop. The S&P 500 has faced pressure from weakness in AI-linked technology stocks, but rotation into other sectors suggests the market's underlying strength is broader than a handful of major names. Investor interest also remains supported by expectations for continued corporate growth.

Risks have not disappeared. Sticky inflation, elevated energy prices, uncertainty around interest rates and concerns over debt-funded AI investment could keep markets unsettled. Even so, easing Treasury yields and signs of recovery across global equities offer support for a mildly bullish U.S. market outlook. Demand tied to AI and cloud investment also remains an important long-term driver. 

With market leadership shifting, investors may benefit from focusing on stocks that consistently outperform the S&P 500. Relative price strength therefore appears to be a useful strategy for identifying stronger opportunities in the current market.

At this stage, investors would be wise to consider companies such as Halozyme Therapeutics HALO, GigaCloud Technology GCT, Lindblad Expeditions Holdings LIND, Permian Resources PR and Chevron Corporation CVX.

Relative Price Strength Strategy

Whether a stock has the potential to offer considerable returns is determined primarily by its earnings and valuation ratios. Simultaneously, it is essential to check whether its price performance exceeds its peers or the industry average.

Upon such comparison, if we find that a stock is unable to match up to wider sectoral growth despite having impressive earnings momentum or valuation multiples, it may be better to avoid it.

However, those outperforming their respective industries or benchmarks should be included in your portfolio since they have a higher chance of securing significant returns. Picking a stock that outperforms its peers ensures a winning option in your hands.

Then again, it is imperative that you determine whether or not an investment has relevant upside potential when considering stocks with significant relative price strength. Stocks delivering better than the S&P 500 for 1 to 3 months, at least, and having solid fundamentals, indicate room for growth and are the best way to go about this strategy.

Finally, it is crucial to find out whether analysts are optimistic about the upcoming earnings of these companies. In order to do this, we have added positive estimate revisions for the current quarter's (Q1) earnings to our screen. When a stock undergoes an upward revision, it leads to additional price gains.
